title: Genetics in medicine: inheritance, mutations and screening
note: Each person carries two copies of most genes, one from each parent. Whether one altered copy is enough (dominant) or both must be altered (recessive), and whether the gene is on an autosome, the X chromosome or mitochondrial DNA, sets the pattern a trait follows through a family.

read.title: Reading a family tree
text: Genetic counselors and physicians often draw a pedigree, a family tree marking who shows a trait. The pattern of affected relatives gives strong clues about how the trait is inherited.

An autosomal dominant trait usually appears in every generation, affects males and females alike, and passes from an affected parent to about half of the children. An autosomal recessive trait often skips generations. Two unaffected parents who each carry one altered copy have a 25 percent chance with each pregnancy of having an affected child, and a 50 percent chance of a child who is an unaffected carrier.

X-linked recessive traits show a sex difference. Because males have only one X chromosome, a single altered copy is enough to affect them, so far more males than females are affected. A father never passes an X-linked variant to his sons, because sons inherit his Y chromosome, but he passes it to every daughter. Mitochondrial traits follow yet another rule: they pass only through mothers, though both sons and daughters can be affected.
Real families are messier. Reduced penetrance and variable expressivity can hide a trait in a carrier, which is why pedigrees are clues, not proof.
